candidates.label: Arabia (Nabataean kingdom, label point)
candidates.support: The label point marks the Nabataean kingdom at its capital, Petra: it is Wikidata's point for the kingdom, about 6 km from Pleiades' point for Petra. How far the New Testament's 'Arabia' matches the kingdom is set out in the history notes.

summary.text: On this map, Arabia is the Nabataean kingdom, also known as Arabia Nabataea: a kingdom with its capital at Petra, ruled by its own kings. In Paul's time it was allied with Rome but was not a Roman province: it became one only when the Roman emperor Trajan annexed it in AD 106. Paul writes that he 'went away into Arabia' and then returned to Damascus, and that in Damascus 'the governor under King Aretas' tried to arrest him.

history.text: The Nabataeans kept their independence as allies of Rome when the Roman general Pompey reorganized the East in 63 BC. Their kingdom had its capital at Petra and reached Bosra in the north and Hegra in the south; its kings included Aretas IV (9 BC - AD 40) and Malichus II (AD 40 - 70/71), who reigned at this project's about AD 50 date. Trajan made it a Roman province in AD 106. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia likewise describes a kingdom with its capital at Petra, allied with the Romans at first and later under their rule.

Galatians 1:17 does not say where in Arabia Paul went, and Paul also writes of 'Mount Sinai in Arabia' (Galatians 4:25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the New Testament uses the name for the Syrian desert or the Sinai peninsula, and it identifies the King Aretas of 2 Corinthians 11:32, whose governor held Damascus when Paul escaped, as an Arabian king. Aretas IV was the Nabataean king from 9 BC to AD 40.

scripture.textWEB: nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia. Then I returned to Damascus.
For this Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and answers to the Jerusalem that exists now, for she is in bondage with her children.

politicalHistory.note: This area's drawn extent includes the Sinai peninsula: the Nabataean kingdom's own towns reached "Rhinocolura (Al-Arish) and Gaza" in the west, Egypt's conventional edge, so Sinai (between the two) falls with this area rather than Egypt.
